title: Same Element, Different Weight
question: How can two atoms be the same element yet differ in mass?
hook: Early radiochemists could not separate some radioactive substances because those substances shared one place in the table.
idea: Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so they share a place in the table and nearly the same chemistry.

beats.prompt: You measure two carbon atoms. Both have six protons, but one has eight neutrons and the other has six. Are they different elements?

choices.label: Yes, the extra neutrons make a new element
choices.feedback: It tempts because the atoms weigh differently, but the proton count decides the element.

choices.label: No, they are isotopes of carbon and share one place in the table
Yes, they must have different numbers of electrons
choices.feedback: It tempts because electrons feel linked to identity, but a neutral atom has as many electrons as protons, so these match.

beats.explain: Atomic number counts protons and identifies the element, so both atoms are carbon with different mass numbers.

beats.prompt: Sort each isotope into its group.
beats.explain: Carbon-12 and carbon-13 are stable, while carbon-14 is radioactive and uranium-235 alpha-decays.

beats.prompt: Match each term to what it means.
pairs: Number of protons in the nucleus
Same atomic number, different mass numbers
A distinct nuclear species of an element
beats.explain: Atomic number counts protons, mass number counts all nucleons, isotopes vary in neutrons, and a nuclide is one distinct nuclear species.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?
steps: Every carbon atom has six protons, so each is carbon.
Carbon-12 has six neutrons and carbon-14 has eight.
So carbon-14 must have a different atomic number from carbon-12.
So the two should sit in different boxes on the periodic table.
beats.explain: Atomic number counts protons, and both have six. Different neutron numbers change the mass number, not the atomic number.
